meta.title: Housing affordability and homelessness, 19 days of posts
meta.subject: housing affordability in Texas — rents and home prices, manufactured and factory-built housing, tiny homes, lot-size and zoning rules, county and city development regulations, NIMBY opposition to new communities, and homelessness policy including encampment bans and housing-first funding
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 19, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas housing affordability, manufactured housing and homelessness, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Cut rules, build more supply
lanes.description: Texas rents and prices are high because zoning, minimum lot sizes, permitting and parking rules block construction, so cities and counties should deregulate and let more homes be built.

lanes.label: Manufactured and tiny homes fix it
lanes.description: Manufactured, modular, factory-built and tiny homes are the fast, cheap route to affordable Texas housing, and rules that restrict them should be loosened.

lanes.label: Blame investors, landlords, developers
lanes.description: Corporate landlords, institutional investors, out-of-state buyers and big developers are driving up Texas rents and home prices and pricing out residents.

lanes.label: Protect neighborhoods, local control
lanes.description: Residents oppose new apartments, subdivisions and manufactured-home communities as threats to neighborhood character, traffic, schools and property values, and defend local and county control over development.

lanes.label: Enforce encampment bans, restore order
lanes.description: Homelessness is a public-safety and disorder problem, so Texas should enforce camping bans, clear encampments and push people into shelter or treatment.

lanes.label: Fund housing-first, not criminalization
lanes.description: Ending homelessness requires funding permanent supportive housing and services, and encampment bans and arrests only move people around without fixing the cause.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

🚨 Law and Order Finally Hits Skid Row

Federal agents and local police did the right thing today by going after the fentanyl and PCP dealers who have treated Skid Row as an open-air market. These traffickers prey on people struggling with addiction and homelessness, trading government benefits for poison while operating out of tents, vehicles, and storefronts. Serving 44 warrants, charging 28 suspects, and taking more than a dozen into custody is exactly the kind of targeted action that disrupts supply and puts criminals on notice.

This is long overdue. Skid Row did not become one of the country’s largest open-air drug markets by accident; years of policies that prioritized tolerance over enforcement allowed gangs and street-level suppliers to dig in. The FBI, DEA, and LAPD are correct to focus on the dealers rather than the addicted, and seizures of drugs, guns, cash, and luxury vehicles show this was organized crime, not petty survival.

Enforcement has to continue. One raid will not clear the market if the same networks simply relocate or if prosecution and sentencing remain weak. Holding traffickers accountable, cutting off the supply of fentanyl and PCP, and pairing arrests with real treatment capacity is the practical path to reducing deaths and restoring basic public order.

posts.name: Selene Mariposa
posts.text:
BOOMERS VS. GEN Z ON HOUSING. I RAN THE MATH. EVERYBODY'S A LITTLE WRONG.

Fox ran a piece today saying Boomers don't understand how hard it is to buy a house. The Boomers say, "I paid 14%!" The kids say, "Yeah, on an $80,000 house!"

Cute fight. Let's do what neither side did. Put rate, price, and income in the same equation.

The question that matters: what share of your paycheck goes to the mortgage? 20% down, 30-year fixed, principal and interest only.

In 1984: $79,900 home. 13.9% rate. $752 a month. That's 40% of median household income.
In 1990: $872 a month. 35%.
In 2000: $997 a month. 28.5%.
In 2010: $919 a month. 22%.
In 2020: $1,132 a month. 20%. The golden age. Free money and lockdown sourdough.
Today: $429,100 home. 7.4% rate. $2,377 a month. 33%.

So, Boomers? You win the "I had it worse" contest on the monthly payment. 40% of your paycheck is brutal. Congratulations. Have a Werther's.

But kids, you win the round that matters most: getting in the door.

In 1984, 20% down was $16,000. About 71% of a year's income.
20% down today is $85,800. About 98% of a year's income.

You can survive a big payment. You can't make a payment on a house you never bought. That down payment is the wall, and it's taller than it's ever been.

Two more things nobody mentions.

Boomers refinanced. Rates fell from 14% to under 7% by 1993, and many cut their payments in half without moving. Today's buyers can do that too if rates drop. "Marry the house, date the rate" is real.

And the article compares a 1984 new-home price to a 2026 existing-home price. That's apples to slightly different apples. Close enough to make the point, but I'm a stickler.

Now let's talk about that $430K "starter home."

$430K is the median. Half the homes sold in America go for less. A starter home is the one you're slightly embarrassed to show your mother-in-law.

At $250,000, the payment at today's rate is $1,385 a month. 19% of median income. Better than 1990, 2000, and 1984. Down payment: $50,000.

Where do $250K houses live? Not Seattle. Not San Diego. Not Austin anymore. Try the Midwest, the South and the parts of Texas where people still wave at you.

And before anybody asks for a new government program, remember who helped build this mess. The National Association of Home Builders found that regulation accounts for about 24% of a new home's price. Roughly $94,000. Permits. Impact fees. Zoning. Lot-size minimums. Energy codes. Each one was "small." Sound familiar, Washington?

More government, more rules, and more fees haven't made houses cheaper. Not once.

The fix needs a calculator and a little compromise.

Start with your income. The old rule says keep housing under about 28% of gross pay. Work backward to the price and rate you can handle, then shop for that house. Not the one on HGTV.

Buy smaller. Your first house doesn't need a theater room and a sixth bathroom.
Look at townhomes and condos.
Look at FHA. You can put down as little as 3.5%. You'll pay mortgage insurance, but you're in, and your payments build equity instead of your landlord's.
Rent out a room. Your college buddy can cover a chunk of the mortgage.
Buy where your paycheck goes further.

So here's my advice to the kids, with love from a mom of four:

If the starter home in your city costs $430K, the house isn't the problem. The zip code is.

Move.

And Boomers, maybe stop bragging about 14%. You bought at 3.6x income and sold to these kids at 4.9x. Somebody made money on that spread, and it wasn't them.

🦋

posts.name: Austin Justice
posts.text:
Austin finally found a homelessness program that shows some promise. Naturally, the City Council wants to hand it to an anti-cop activists to stop it.

No Wrong Door is a program where cops trained in crisis response team up with medics and caseworkers to deal with the small group of people who keep showing up in 911 calls, jail and the ER, mostly homeless and mentally ill.

The early results, from the city itself, shows the highest-risk people in the program had 57% fewer crisis calls. And the officers running it haven't arrested a single client.

That wasn't good enough for the activist class. A few weeks ago, the ACLU, the Texas Civil Rights Project, public defenders and harm reduction groups demanded Austin pull police out of the program, or bury them in new rules, like requiring defense lawyers be notified before an officer can even talk to some participants, thus eliminating any means to actually help them in a crisis.

One week later, Council Member José Velásquez proposed a new "community advisory group" to help steer the program's policies and operations. He listed who should be on it: the ACLU, the Texas Civil Rights Project, the public defenders, the harm reduction alliance. 

Council Member Marc Duchen asked aptly why the city would build an advisory board out of the program's loudest critics. He lost 3-1. Velásquez, Vanessa Fuentes and Ryan Alter voted yes.

The full Council votes October 22.

A police-led program might actually be getting people off the streets and out of jail, and Austin's response is to invite the city's most anti-police groups in to take it over and make sure cops can't do their job.
